column2: A second group of prints: drypoints exploring the lively movement of the line (Velocidad).
A second group of prints: drypoints freely exploring the living movement of the line.

Despite difficulties raising the funds for a building designed by Gropius (classrooms and individual studies), the college moves to the new site; the construction of the Studies Building itself becomes part of the program. A building designed by Gropius, classrooms and individual studies Consequences: The college pursues its educational and communal odyssey at Lake Eden until 1956

Rice resigns from the leadership, but his egalitarian educational principles remain a force that permeates the college, sometimes muted, a source of factions and conflicts, taken up or modified by his successors. Consequences: His vision remains vital and generative for almost all of the college's twenty-three years of existence
Rice is forced to cut his ties with the college, mainly because of his own failings, according to his grandson. Consequences: Rice then devotes himself to writing
Rice leaves the college; he and Albers part in a noisy silence — Albers, who always tells the truth, cannot say both that he is sorry and that he is glad

Kocher, a “modern” architect, former head of the architecture department at the University of Virginia and then editor of The Architectural Record, offered to come and teach architecture while incorporating the design of the buildings (a special salary obtained through the Carnegie Corporation's “Visiting Artist” program). Richard Gothe, a German worker with a doctorate in economics, a former director of summer work camps for the American Friends Service Committee, convinced the community of what student labor could accomplish — he was hired to teach economics and direct the program (too autocratic for American students, he got them started before being replaced). Charlie Godfrey, a local contractor who had built a large hotel in Montreat and had long been out of work, agreed to teach construction to the students; he demanded a qualified professional assistant, laying out the work each morning for the afternoon student crews. Godfrey directed most of the trades: stone and concrete masonry, welding, carpentry, plumbing, electrical work; a hotel in Montreat, a Southern Presbyterian resort Consequences: the self-building begins

Since no one wanted to lead the fund-raising, Dreier proposed starting the foundations, photographing the progress, and showing the photos to potential donors. While Europe wondered whether the democracies could compete with the dictatorships, the college presented itself as a small democracy able to mobilize in a crisis — and did so.

In the fall of 1940, as the program was getting under way, Dreier was invited to dinner at the White House with Mr. and Mrs. Roosevelt and some twenty guests; after dinner, he talked and showed photos of BMC students and teachers at work to those who had not gone back to work with the president. some twenty guests Consequences: no direct money, but a boost in morale that helped carry the work through

A summer program started almost at once at Lake Eden: a “work camp” with several courses, including one in architecture. A cottage was given to Larry Kocher and his family and to several other faculty members. By the end of the summer, the large Studies Building had been designed, the insulation of the summer buildings begun, and the farm well under way, supplying all the dairy products. the farm supplied all the dairy products

When the program is launched the following fall, the narrator is invited to dinner at the White House with Mr. and Mrs. Roosevelt and some twenty other guests; after dinner, he talks and shows photos of BMC students and teachers at work to those who had not withdrawn to work with the president. about twenty guests; photos of students and faculty at work Consequences: No direct money, but a boost in morale that helped carry the project through

A summer program starts almost at once at Lake Eden in the form of a “work camp” with several summer courses, including one in architecture; a cottage is assigned to Larry Kocher and his family and to other teachers. a cottage for the Kocher family and other teachers

After a series of small disasters as a brakeman on passenger trains, the railroad officials suggest that he find work elsewhere; the passenger trainmaster hands him a pass to North Carolina and firmly closes his office door. A railroad pass provided; the trainmaster's sigh. Consequences: The start of the most astonishing year of his life.

The five-year lease with the Blue Ridge Assembly expires in June 1941; Dr. Weatherford, its head, hints that he plans to open a girls' school in Lee Hall in the fall of 1941. Worried, the college writes in the spring of 1940 to its friends around the country asking them to look out for other sites: the Middle West is rather ruled out and the Deep South certainly; the first choice is to stay in North Carolina, but it is prepared to consider elsewhere. Nothing as attractive as Lake Eden emerges. the lease expiring in June 1941; a girls' school planned in Lee Hall Consequences: The decision to move to Lake Eden with scaled-down plans.

The college turns to A. Lawrence Kocher, a former professor of architecture at the University of Virginia and Carnegie Tech and a former editor of the Architectural Record, to design a single study building: downstairs, classrooms, weaving, and storage; upstairs, student studies and a few faculty apartments. Gropius and Breuer recommend Kocher and agree to advise him, but are somewhat piqued that the college went to another architect rather than asking them for a simplified version. Consequences: The plans become affordable.
A local man of good reputation is hired as contractor for the study building.
The postmistress's husband, chiefly responsible for maintenance at Lee Hall, takes on greater responsibility as head carpenter.
Several students from the Harvard School of Architecture come down to Black Mountain; several stay, including two Thais immediately nicknamed Nim and Nik. nicknames given at once

A German refugee, a doctor of economics from Berlin and a master toolmaker, who had taken part in the work camps of the Weimar Republic, organizes the volunteer crews of students and teachers into specialties and imposes daily schedules to be strictly followed. named crews: “rock-gathering,” “cement-mixing” Consequences: the structure of the building site

A handsome New Englander of thirty: she assists Albers in the art courses, teaches woodworking, designs furniture, runs the farm; she becomes a kind of community arbiter, admired for her integrity and frankness. thirty when she arrived

One night two malcontents post a notice on the bulletin board asking for zombies for the work program, in reaction to the folk songs on the way to the building site and to the mystique of salvation through physical labor embodied by Dreier. a nighttime notice on the bulletin board Consequences: tongue-clucking and rage in the community

After the Nazi invasion, Madame and Natasha cross France on foot under strafing by the Luftwaffe to take ship for Morocco; Madame protects a hatbox containing her finest hat, kept from prerevolutionary Russia. A hatbox clutched to her stomach, almost daily strafing Consequences: A stay in Morocco during the first years of the war

In the 1940s in Washington, Olson proudly shows Connie, at the breakfast table, a magazine open to one of his first poems; she answers indifferently “I'll look at it later” and sets the magazine aside. Olson is crushed by this and never forgets it; he still speaks of it to Mary Fiore years later at Black Mountain. a story told to Rumaker by Mary Fiore Consequences: a lasting wound; Rumaker possibly reads in it a healthy gesture of resistance by Connie, a need for Jungian individuation in the face of Charles's gigantic appetite

From the 1940s on, the two couples (de Kooning and Pollock) vie for fortune and fame; the wives wage a war of influence, Elaine maneuvering through others, Lee attacking head-on. Consequences: The wives' rivalry feeds and sustains the painters' rivalry.

By the early 1940s, Albers has assembled a collection of papers that he brings to class in a large suitcase. A student remembers: they rummaged in this grab bag of scraps to find what they needed — it was dramatic and fun; in the search itself, something happened. a large suitcase of papers

A snapshot of Eddie Dreier, son of Theodore and Barbara Dreier, taken in 1940 when they all shared a house at Black Mountain College, is the evident starting point of a small humorous drypoint titled Eh-De a house shared at the college; title of the print: Eh-De
Gropius encourages the Graduate School of Design to recruit Albers, who receives a job offer in 1940 but turns it down. Consequences: Albers stays at Black Mountain.

Being Jewish, Wildenhain must flee, first to the Netherlands and then to the United States, where she arrives in 1940 and becomes the country's preeminent Bauhaus ceramist. Consequences: Her later refusal of the post at Black Mountain

Lacking the means for the Gropius-Breuer project, the college turns to Kocher, who proposes a single structure with four wings radiating from a central hall; he settles at Black Mountain in the fall of 1940 to direct the construction of the first wing, the only one ever built. Untrained labor, limited resources Consequences: The birth of the Studies Building and of the design-build program

Olson and Shahn meet in the early 1940s at the Office of War Information, where they produce a bilingual brochure to rally Spanish speakers behind the war. brochure titled Spanish-Speaking Americans in the War (1943) Consequences: the start of a long friendship

Workers at the vast brickworks of Tlatilco uncover extraordinarily rich Preclassic tombs, revealing the site's figurines to the world of collectors. hundreds upon hundreds of tombs crammed with figurines, sophisticated pottery, red hematite, and pieces of imported asphalt Consequences: Never before had such a rich and refined Preclassic site been known; the figurines enter collections from the early 1940s.

Three weeks on the road across the Midwest when Terry buys a 1940 Chevrolet; he confronts, new to it, a public tied to the roads, reassesses his regional prejudices, and sees for the first time changes and similarities. Three weeks; a 1940 Chevrolet

In the summer of 1940, the college learns that it has only one year left on the Blue Ridge site; the campus plans drawn by Gropius and Breuer (1939 model) must be abandoned. The faculty turns to A. Lawrence Kocher for buildings the community can build with a local contractor. Gropius and Breuer's 1939 model for Lake Eden (not built). Consequences: Construction of the Studies Building begins in the fall of 1940.

The faculty member Molly Gregory and the student Alex Reed build the Quiet House, a small square fieldstone building, in memory of Eddie Dreier, the Dreiers' son, killed in a car accident on campus. a small square fieldstone structure, thick walls, narrow slit windows, set against the mountain in a grove of wild greenery, beside the dirt path between the dining hall and the Studies Building; damp and musty in every season Consequences: in the 1950s, no one uses it anymore for prayer and meditation; it becomes a place for nighttime erotic trysts

Toward the end of his stay at Black Mountain, in the late 1940s, Albers begins the Variant series: countless oils in similar formats in which only the color changes. Consequences: Directly anticipates the Homages to the Square

Olson and Dahlberg, both in Gloucester, work hard and share their meals. Olson's mother, calling Charles her “growing boy,” gives him a plate heaped with fried chicken and serves Dahlberg a warmed-over pork chop. A dish of fried chicken piled high against a single leftover pork chop Consequences: Dahlberg, furious, writes to Olson that he has deplorable manners; he will still refer to it in a letter to John Cech dated January 27, 1972

A typewritten letter: basketball at Hobey's, Abbott & Costello jokes, Pepsi-Cola, “all the colonels are in the army,” signed with a row of O's: “these things stand for love”. basketball, popcorn, jokes, repeated O's

A handwritten letter to his father in the hospital (which his mother does not know about): grades of 80-90 in arithmetic, a horse named Don at Hooey's sister's, flash photos dressed up as a ghost in a sheet, the baseball glove lent to all the kids. 90s or 80s in arithmetic, 3 flashbulbs, a sheet and a mask, a baseball glove

In a speech full of allusions to the war against fascism in Europe, Albers declares that freedom “from” something has no positive meaning; only freedom “for” something is active and productive. Consequences: Anticipates by eighteen years Isaiah Berlin's distinction between the two freedoms, but in reverse.

The architect Lawrence Kocher designs Black Mountain's second campus (Lake Eden) and helps build it in 1940; he had earlier collaborated with Albert Frey on influential prefabricated houses, including the Aluminaire (1931), and published texts on prefabrication in Architectural Record. Aluminaire, 1931; a series of articles in Architectural Record

Early in 1940, less than seven years after the opening, the faculty asks Rice to resign; he will never return to higher education Rice is then 52 Consequences: A final departure from teaching; a second career as a writer

The resignation brings great relief but little rejoicing. The college loses a certain paternal leadership and a charismatic presence while gaining normality. Rice was domineering, inflexible, cynical, insensitive to those for whom academic life means collegiality and cordiality — but also brilliant, innovative, open, involved, driven not by long-term ambition but by a daily curiosity about people. He held court in the vast lobby of Lee Hall, a great manipulator or a great listener; he knew how to drive others into a fury and seemed to enjoy testing that power; but he did not understand why colleagues, students, and his wife had come to have enough of it, and wrongly concluded that the problem lay with them. The “cavernous” lobby of Lee Hall as a theater.

Commissioned by Grace and Edwin Denby, he designs costumes and sets for Nini Theilade's ballet Les Nuages at the Metropolitan Opera House; fashion illustrations for Harper's Bazaar. The same year, his friend Arshile Gorky paints two pictures titled Pirate.
Anni's mother, lucky enough to have fled Nazi Germany, is reduced to waiting on tables, she who once rang for the butler and the cook.
Two posthumous exhibitions in private New York galleries follow Klee's death; Time sees in them a body of work of quiet, pastel-tinted insanity.

Christopher Morley gives financial support to Fuller's Dymaxion Deployment Unit project — an adaptation of corrugated-steel grain bins for emergency housing — with the earnings from his novel Kitty Foyle. A corrugated-steel bin; financed by the receipts from Kitty Foyle. Consequences: One of the rare cases of patronage in Fuller's career, otherwise his own boss.

On the recommendation of Reginald Marsh, who admires his drawing, Kline covers the walls of a Greenwich Village tavern with pencil portraits of the regulars, at 50 cents apiece; elsewhere he paints murals of burlesque queens for another bar and a panorama of the region for the American Legion hall in Lehighton. 50 cents a portrait
In the early 1940s, he spends long months copying El Greco's View of Toledo, a passionate inquiry that yields a tense and fresh commentary on that sublime painting.

Graham, seeing the painting in progress, finds it tremendous; Bill says he would let it go for fifty dollars; Graham comes back half an hour later with the money. The painting is saved, still wet on the easel, while Bill was irritated with it. Consequences: The rent (35 dollars) is paid, with 15 dollars left for meals; the painting still exists.

After long meetings linking the Rice problem to the college's financial precariousness, the Board decides that the future cannot be staked on his presence: too many outside problems to afford a major internal difficulty; Rice has made great promises and has not kept them. a private letter from Wunsch Consequences: Another mission by Wunsch to Southern Pines, with Nell Rice.

A month before Rice's resignation, the faculty commissions the former Bauhaus architects Walter Gropius and Marcel Breuer to design the main buildings of the new Lake Eden campus. Consequences: The founder's departure coincides with the beginning of the second campus, six miles and at least a hundred years from the first.

The composer plays her the sound of a manipulated kiss that roars like a lion; then the tour of five Italian ice-cream parlors that she laughingly calls a binge Atmosphere: Sensual and paternal play; sonic wonder Stakes: A young woman's initiation into the world of avant-garde men

Dreier dines with the Roosevelts and some twenty guests; after dinner, while some withdraw to work with the president, he shows photographs of BMC students and teachers at work on the Lake Eden building site. Atmosphere: an intimate evening of power, the pride of a treasurer-laborer Stakes: the survival of a small college displayed at the summit of the state

While the community sings folk songs on the way to the building site and lives in the communion of the committed, two opponents pin up a notice at night asking for zombies for the work program. Words: “Wanted: zombies for the work program” Atmosphere: nighttime sabotage, black humor against the collective euphoria Stakes: the first crack in the unity of the building site

Charles proudly shows the magazine open to his poem; Connie: “I'll look at it later,” and she pushes the magazine aside; Charles is crushed; years later he still tells Mary Fiore about it, the wound still raw Words: “I'll look at it later” Atmosphere: breakfast, an indifference that kills Stakes: a founding wound of the couple; a gesture of resistance by Connie, according to Rumaker

Grace shows her early work; Bill tells her she has modern art all wrong and proposes that she do what he has Elaine do: a perfect still-life drawing that he tears up before making her start again Words: “Vell, I tell Elaine to use the finest pencil in the world... I tear it up and I tell her to do it again” Stakes: the master's harshness and the submission of the student-lover
A casual snapshot of little Eddie in the shared house; it will become a humorous drypoint titled Eh-De Atmosphere: Everyday family life at the college, humor

Graham comes in and admires Seated Figure in progress; Bill says he would let it go for fifty dollars; Graham goes out and comes back within half an hour with the bills; Bill, caught off guard but annoyed with the painting and pressed for the rent, accepts. Words: Bill: for fifty dollars, it is his. Graham: he will be right back. Atmosphere: A bohemian studio atmosphere, cash on the nail, a canvas still soaking wet. Stakes: A painting survives only if it leaves the studio.

Wunsch comes to get the resignation; Rice, determined not to let him make the request, forces him to overstay his time; Wunsch visibly struggles with himself, then leaves without speaking frankly; he then writes a courteous letter. Words: Wunsch by letter: he fully enjoyed the visit and found Rice calm, friendly, and wise, with something of the old spirit. Atmosphere: Muffled tension, a silent struggle on both sides. Stakes: Whether or not to obtain the founder's resignation.

Rice sets his conditions: he will not come back unless invited by the Board, nor unless he can persuade Nell to take him back; if she is through with him, he is through with teaching. He proposes to finish his book by December, to live in the stone house all fall, to come to the college for the evening meal every day, and to teach a single class three times a week. Wunsch replies that the Board would rather close at once than after another internal struggle. Rice: he wants to come back to prove to them that he is a changed man; he wants to redeem himself. He predicts that if he resigns, the college will be inert within two years. Nell intervenes several times, listing his broken promises and refusing to tie herself to him again. Rice weeps twice and leaves the room, then the house, saying he has been repudiated by his wife and by the college. No raised voices, but insidious remarks about his colleagues' weaknesses. Rice's concrete proposal: the stone house, a daily evening meal, one class three times a week Consequences: Wunsch leaves once again without a resignation; Rice promises to write within a few days.

The Board waits a week; no resignation arrives; it sends the formal request. Mangold writes to Dreier (visiting Cambridge) that he doubts it will be obtained easily: Rice will no doubt want a prior financial agreement and a high estimate of his share in any liquidation. Consequences: Rice, out of excessive pride, sends his resignation by return mail, to the Board's surprise.

The letter of resignation is shown to the faculty and the student officers; the wording of the public announcement and a fair financial settlement are discussed. Anne Mangold reports that everyone's attitude is excellent, without triumphalism, and that the saying that if Rice disappeared everyone would be ready to try anything is coming true 100 percent. Consequences: A palace revolution accomplished: the sons are on the throne.

Delicate verbal negotiations determine that the college will pay Rice until the end of the academic year, pay unspecified sums directly to Swarthmore for Mary Rice's tuition, and recognize Rice's interest in the Lake Eden property should the college close and sell its land. Several thousand volumes left on indefinite loan to the college library: the great classics, rare eighteenth-century manuscripts collected for his research on Swift, and a first edition of the Oxford New English Dictionary. Consequences: Rice leaves the college with a thin financial safety net.

Rice states his conditions (a return only if he is wanted and if Nell comes back), proposes his plan (the stone house, daily dinners, one class a week), then struggles: he wants to redeem himself; Nell cites his broken promises; Rice weeps twice and leaves the room, then the house; he comes back: the college needs him; Wunsch urges him to choose writing. Words: Rice: he has been repudiated by his wife and by the college; he wants to come back to prove that he is a changed man; a prediction of an inert college within two years. Atmosphere: No shouting or storms, but tears, exits from the house, insidious remarks. Stakes: The fate of the founder and, he says, of the college itself.

Elaine probably persuades the shy Bill to try work as a fashion illustrator through Rudy Burckhardt and Harper's Bazaar. She models for him for a series of sketches of hairstyles published in the March 1940 issue, at $75 a sketch — a generous sum. The art director Alexey Brodovitch will not take any more. $75 a sketch, March 1940 issue

Ten days after the resignation, Wunsch comes back with Nell to settle the details. The meeting begins with a tirade from Rice (this action slams the door in his face; he fears he will not be able to live by his pen and that no college will employ him after his expulsion). Wunsch concedes that the public announcement will simply say that he is leaving to devote himself to writing. The tension subsides; Rice calms down, smokes his pipe, and warns them not to cut off the heads of the best as well as the worst to make the place comfortable for the mediocre. Then cocktails, a dinner of broiled steak, mushrooms, and artichokes; conversation about New Harmony, Brook Farm, the causes of their failure, the need for a central critical intelligence in every college, the power of mysticism in a leader. Finally, finances: Rice hopes to finish his book without the pressure of looking for work, having to support himself and a daughter in college. cocktails; broiled steak, mushrooms, artichokes; Rice's pipe Consequences: A fair agreement seems possible; the evening ends on a relatively kindly note.

The resignation is made public in the form Rice preferred. He shares the general lot of the faculty: the same percentage of salary until the end of the academic year, then, in the following first term, a small monthly allowance sufficient for food and lodging, with the assurance that his daughter's tuition will be covered. a monthly allowance for food and lodging; the daughter's tuition covered Consequences: The founder's final departure.

BMC Newsletter no. 7 (March 1940) announces the resignation; picked up by Newsweek (April 15, 1940, p. 43). A financial arrangement negotiated in letters between Steinau and Rice, March-May 1940. Consequences: The official end of the Rice-BMC tie

The meeting opens with a tirade (Rice feels driven out and fears for his professional future); Wunsch concedes control of the public announcement; Rice relaxes, smokes his pipe, and warns against beheading the best as well as the worst; cocktails, a dinner of broiled steak with mushrooms and artichokes; a long conversation about New Harmony, Brook Farm, the mysticism of the leader; finally the finances, on a kindly note. Words: Rice: this action slams the door in his face; take care not to cut off the heads of the best and the worst to make the place comfortable for the mediocre; Wunsch to him: why on earth does he want to go back and live with those pitiful people? — The college needs him. Atmosphere: From anger to a warm unity: pipe, cocktails, ideas, dinner. Stakes: Settling the founder's departure with dignity.

The YMCA, delayed with its girls' school, granted one more year. The college organized a building program at Lake Eden with its own hands: $3,000 that could be saved beyond current expenses (faculty salaries suspended, only small payments according to pressing needs), for a Farmall tractor ($1,000) and a carload of cement ($2,000), in order to begin the foundations of a large study building on the lakeshore. The plan was then to insulate and heat the dining hall, two dormitory lodges, and cottages. The idea seemed at first impossible and ridiculous, but there was a month left to build a plausible program — it was May. $3,000: Farmall tractor $1,000, carload of cement $2,000; the previous winter: two weeks of below-zero temperatures Consequences: the launch of the work camp and the Studies Building

Three days before the German army's triumphal entry into Paris, Albers, before a group of potential donors to Black Mountain College, makes a rare political statement against the war and urges his audience to cherish their freedom: only spiritual goods are lasting and worth saving.

Mary and Frank drive with their father to the summer cottage of their stepmother, Launa Darnell Rice, taking the dachshund Nicky; a night in Asheville, where Frank runs into Ann Craig Sutton, whom he had known in Havana with the American Friends Service Committee. The dachshund Nicky; a chance meeting in Asheville with enormous consequences. Consequences: Frank proposes to Ann by letter; she comes to Bella Vista in August.

On the way to Bella Vista with his father, his sister, and the dachshund Nicky, Frank happens upon Ann Craig Sutton, whom he had known in Havana. Atmosphere: Romantic chance. Stakes: Enormous consequences: the 1941 wedding and the last meeting of Rice's parents.

Gropius and Breuer are miffed that the college is hesitating; Dreier corresponds with Kocher on July 8, 11, and 17, 1940; Kocher's daughter describes her father's consultation with Gropius and Breuer. Consequences: Kocher becomes the architect of the Studies Building

Klee dies in July 1940, shortly after turning sixty, from the effects of scleroderma. Less than a year after his 60th birthday Consequences: Schlemmer records his admiration in his diary and worries about the fate of abstract art in a Europe increasingly hostile to modernism

On learning of Klee's death, Schlemmer writes in his diary what a marvelous visual and spiritual contribution he made, what wisdom; then he wonders whether abstract art, in a Europe increasingly inhospitable to modernism, will still find leaders and a refuge.

End of summer: plans for the large Studies Building completed, insulation of the summer buildings begun for winter use, the farm supplying all the dairy products and most of the college's meat; everything is ready, except the money, to begin construction. the farm supplies all the dairy products and most of the meat

John Andrew Rice's relentless Socratic challenges at table end up sending Ann Sutton away in tears; an affectionate relationship between father-in-law and daughter-in-law will be established only later.

Ann, who has come to visit Frank after his proposal by letter, sits down to her first dinner with the Rice family; the father subjects the young fiancée to a barrage of Socratic challenges until she leaves the table in tears. Atmosphere: Stifling intellectual tension, tears at table. Stakes: The father's ordeal imposed on his future daughter-in-law; reconciliation deferred.

One Friday afternoon, just after the site has been drained and the foundation trenches dug, ready to receive concrete the following Monday, pockets of mud are discovered that require driving piles; buying a pile driver is impossible, the college can hardly pay for food. The narrator, an engineer himself, takes Charlie back to the site and leaves him to think, then returns to Blue Ridge in the darkest perplexity about what to tell the hopeful students. discovered on a Friday afternoon; concrete pouring planned for Monday; the drive back to Blue Ridge Consequences: The building program threatened with a halt

On Saturday evening, Charlie calls the narrator and shows him the plan of a homemade pile driver powered by the Farmall tractor: a double tower twenty-seven feet high (in two-by-twelve rafters) with vertical guide rails, mounted on wooden skids straddling the trenches; a 500-pound black-gum log that will not split is hauled to the top by a steel cable wound on a wide-flanged pulley designed for the tractor's power takeoff; the clutch is released, the pulley spins free, and the log drops twenty-seven feet in free fall. The narrator, an engineer, sees that Charlie knows what he is talking about. a 27-foot (~8.2 m) tower in 2x12s; a 500-pound (~227 kg) black-gum log; a 27-foot free fall; steel cable; a pulley on the Farmall's power takeoff Consequences: Monday's program is revised: students and teachers sent into the forest to cut piles instead of pouring concrete

On learning of the solution, the students are elated: only two weeks' delay while Charlie builds the machine and begins driving the piles they cut. All the piles are driven, all the foundations poured, the wooden frame raised at great speed so that something stands above the ground; the photos are taken north, to the White House, to show potential backers, the money is brought back, materials are bought, and the cycle begins again. an estimated two weeks' delay Consequences: Larry and Charlie direct the work, in effect teaching

Kocher moves to the college full-time: he takes part every day in the construction from his own plans and teaches courses in architecture and design. Consequences: the building site attracts students from the Harvard School of Architecture, including two Thais who stay on at the college

Harper's publishes Rice's recollections of his paternal grandmother's house, in which he unleashes his contempt without sparing the women, describing “Grandmother Rice” as a vegetable, nailed to her split-bottom chair in the corner by the fireplace. A split-bottom chair, the fireplace corner, beans to string, potatoes to peel, Aunt Mollie in the kitchen.

Friday afternoon: the site is drained, the trenches ready for concrete on Monday. Pockets of mud are discovered: piles are needed, and thus an unaffordable machine. The narrator brings Charlie to the site, leaves him to ponder, and drives back down to Blue Ridge weighing the worst dilemma of his life; what to tell the students, full of hope and “rarin' to go”? Words: Interior monologue: what to tell the students brimming with hope? Atmosphere: A dismal Friday evening and Saturday morning Stakes: The survival of the building program and of the college's morale

On Saturday evening, Charlie telephones; the narrator goes down to his house; Charlie shows the plan of the pile driver: a double tower twenty-seven feet high in two-by-twelves, wooden skids, steel cable, a pulley on the Farmall's power takeoff, a 500-pound black-gum log in a free fall of twenty-seven feet. The narrator, an engineer, sees that it will work. Words: Charlie is sure that a twenty-seven-foot drop will be enough to drive any pile Atmosphere: Relief, inventive urgency Stakes: The work resumes on Monday — differently

Monday's program is changed: instead of pouring concrete, everyone who was to work in the afternoon goes up into the forest to cut piles. On learning the news and the plan, they are elated: only two weeks' delay, the time it takes Charlie to build the machine and begin driving the piles they cut. Atmosphere: Collective elation Stakes: Hope returns

Sarton, in a letter to Rosalind Greene, describes the trucks going down the mountain every afternoon filled with teachers and students, and Straus, a German psychiatrist with a fine white head, tossing stones to a girl who passes them to a boy who sets them in the wall prepared with cement. She helped with the wall one afternoon and felt more whole for it.
After Sarton's lecture on Yeats, a student spent an entire week of “interlude” (a declared period of work without classes) studying the books by Yeats that Sarton had brought.

Sarton read a long poem on freedom, bad but provocative, which was discussed at length; she criticized their lack of homage and of religious awe, the insufficiency of silence; the college met her bold criticism with an excellent impersonal discussion.

Four months after Klee's death, Time characterizes his work as childish scribbles, artistic babble; the unsigned article mentions the American collections and notes that American connoisseurs paid 750 dollars a canvas for his ectoplasmic scratchings — a direct reference to Edward Warburg's purchases, whose prices are understated by 50 dollars by mistake. $750 per canvas according to Time (an error: $50 less than the actual figure); the Willard and Buchholz galleries in New York Consequences: The broad American public discovers Klee through this caricature; the article also reports Gropius's invitation to the Bauhaus and mocks Hitler and degenerate art

Every afternoon, trucks going down the mountain filled with teachers and students; on the building site, white-haired Straus tosses stones to a girl who passes them to a boy who sets them in the wall with cement; Sarton helps with the wall one afternoon. Words: “Rosalind, it is a great sight…” Atmosphere: The joy of shared work, almost religious Stakes: Utopia in action

In the summer of 1941, back in the United States, Josef begins a long series of pen-and-ink drawings, later translated into zincographs, evoking the ancient temples of Mexico; titles: Santuario, A Monte Albán.
